cards.title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(N\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(N+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.
cards.definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. Membership in [P](definitions.html#p-np) uses the shared uniform bit-cost convention. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm{P}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.
cards.why: ARRIVAL isolates the complexity of a finite deterministic process with one bit of memory at each switch. Its outcome has short verifiable evidence on both sides, but a general efficient decision algorithm would need to go beyond following the potentially exponential trajectory.

cards.context:
The local rule is elementary, but a vertex remembers which of its two arcs should be used next. With n vertices there are 2ⁿ possible switch configurations in addition to the token position. Long deterministic runs therefore do not contradict the small size of the graph. Ordinary reachability ignores these switch settings and does not decide which sink the token actually reaches.

The source gives short verifiable certificates for both answers using switching flows: counts of traversals that obey conservation and alternation. This places the decision problem in NP ∩ coNP. Certificates can establish the outcome without listing an exponentially long trajectory, but their existence does not itself provide a polynomial-time way to find them.

The 2021 algorithm runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) time and becomes polynomial when deleting a fixed number of vertices makes the graph acyclic. The former is a general improvement over direct simulation; the latter keeps a structural restriction. Neither is the all-instance polynomial bound asked for here.

The 2025 work gives a bound \(2^{O(k\log^2 n)}\) for treewidth \(k\), which is quasipolynomial, not polynomial, even when \(k\) is fixed. It also relates ARRIVAL to approximate fixed points of contractions in the ℓ₁ metric. The paper explicitly distinguishes polynomially many function evaluations from a polynomial total running time.

The 2026 paper proves polynomial time for binary ladders: simple switch graphs with exactly two vertices at each occupied distance level from the two sinks. Such graphs can frustrate earlier algorithms, so solving them is meaningful progress. The restriction concerns the shortest-distance layers of the graph and is not satisfied by general instances.

A polynomial-time algorithm would settle a basic deterministic process whose YES and NO answers already have efficiently checked evidence. A lower bound excluding all such algorithms would be a major complexity separation; the difficulty of simulating the process is only one part of that question.

cards.title: Recognizing good-for-games and good-for-MDP automata
cards.formal: Determine the exact worst-case computational complexity of each of the following two recognition languages: \[\mathrm{GFG}_{\mathrm{par}}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-games parity automaton}\},\qquad \mathrm{GFM}_{\mathrm B}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-MDP Büchi automaton}\}.\] The input is an explicit finite nondeterministic automaton, and the number of parity priorities is unbounded and part of the first input. The requested classification is for each language separately, with matching complexity-class upper and hardness bounds under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The source's two recognition tasks are retained; no particular class membership conjecture is substituted for either classification.
cards.definitions:
An automaton has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), an initial state \(q_0\), and a complete transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\). Completeness means that every state and letter admit a transition; a rejecting sink handles missing transitions. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\) follows transitions \((q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\) from \(q_0\). A parity automaton has a map \(p:\Delta\to\mathbb N\) and accepts a run when the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A Büchi automaton has a marked set \(F\subseteq\Delta\) and accepts a run when transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often. Its language \(L(\mathcal A)\) contains the words with some accepting run. A good-for-games (GFG) automaton admits a single deterministic rule that selects each next transition using only the finite input prefix read so far, so that its induced run accepts every \(w\in L(\mathcal A)\). The rule may remember the entire past; it cannot inspect future letters. One rule must work on all words.

A finite Markov decision process (MDP) over \(\Sigma\) has finite state and action sets \(S,U\), an initial state \(s_0\), a nonempty set \(U(s)\) of enabled actions at each state, a label \(\ell(s,u)\in\Sigma\), and a distribution \(P(s,u,\cdot)\) on \(S\) for each enabled pair. Distribution entries are real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. A policy maps the observed finite history of states and actions to a distribution on the enabled actions. It generates a path by choosing \(u_i\), emitting \(\ell(s_i,u_i)\), and sampling \(s_{i+1}\) using \(P\); products of these conditional probabilities give the path measure. Define \[V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)=\sup_\pi\Pr_M^\pi[\ell(s_0,u_0)\ell(s_1,u_1)\cdots\in L(\mathcal A)].\] In the product with \(\mathcal A\), a policy observes the joint state \((s_i,q_i)\), chooses an enabled pair consisting of \(u_i\) and a transition \((q_i,\ell(s_i,u_i),q_{i+1})\), then samples \(s_{i+1}\) from \(P(s_i,u_i,\cdot)\). Thus the automaton choice precedes that next random state and sees no future. Let \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)\) be the supremum, over all such history-dependent randomized product policies, of the probability that the selected automaton run satisfies its Büchi condition. The automaton is good-for-MDP (GFM) if \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)=V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)\) for every finite MDP over its alphabet and every initial MDP state. The product policy may depend on the MDP. This is exact equality of probabilities, without approximation or a probability-one promise.

Only the automaton is input to recognition; MDPs, policies and GFG rules are quantified objects. States, letters and transitions are explicitly enumerated; indices and priorities use binary integers with delimiters. Input size \(n\) is the total bit length, and invalid descriptions are rejected. The alphabet size, graph size and number of priorities are not fixed parameters. Computational bounds use uniform Turing machines and worst-case resource use over inputs of length at most \(n\), with exact acceptance and no randomized error. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(X\) to \(Y\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) with \(x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y\). A language is \(\mathcal C\)-complete if it belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and every language in \(\mathcal C\) reduces to it in this sense. Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np), [PSPACE](definitions.html#space) and [EXP, also called EXPTIME](definitions.html#exponential-time).
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked matching complexity classifications for both recognition languages with the specified explicit input encoding and reduction convention. For each claimed complete class \(\mathcal C\), prove the resource upper bound and \(\mathcal C\)-hardness. Any other class used in the answer must have an independent machine/resource or logical definition, not a definition that merely renames this recognition problem or the collection of problems reducible to it. The precision requested is complexity-class completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions, not an exact leading constant in running time. An isolated improvement of one bound, an algorithm requiring a fixed priority count, or a result only for one recognition language is partial progress. Numerical approximation of the MDP values is not the acceptance criterion.
cards.why: These recognition problems measure the cost of checking whether a compact nondeterministic specification supports composition with an adversarial system or with a probabilistic controller. Their semantic definitions quantify over infinitely many behaviors, although their inputs are finite graphs. Matching classifications would explain the computational price of certifying these useful restrictions on nondeterminism and the difference between their game and probabilistic settings.

cards.context:
Existence of an accepting run is a hindsight property: a nondeterministic automaton can have a successful branch for each word without any single online method selecting those branches. GFG demands such a uniform method. The input automaton is not promised to have the property; recognizing whether it does is the task.

GFM asks a different compositional question. An MDP describes both choices controlled by a policy and transitions sampled from fixed distributions. Its semantic objective only asks that the generated word have some accepting run. Its product objective also requires choosing that run as the word is produced. The second probability cannot exceed the first, and GFM requires equality for every finite MDP.

The policy in the product may be designed for the particular MDP, observing its current state and its past behavior. GFG instead requires one prefix-based resolution valid for every input word. This distinction makes GFM more permissive; it does not turn the two recognition languages into the same problem.

The 2-token theorem settles a major structural characterization of GFG parity automata and yields polynomial-time recognition at each fixed priority count. It does not yield one polynomial-time bound uniform in the number of priorities. The CONCUR survey records NP-hardness and PSPACE membership. The LICS paper gives the matching NP upper bound.

GFM Büchi recognition is already decidable, with a PSPACE hardness lower bound and an EXPTIME algorithm. Consequently the missing result is a matching complexity classification, not an existence proof for some terminating algorithm. The source proves that a qualitative version based on probability-one preservation agrees with its quantitative GFM property, but the card states the original full-probability definition.

The interpretation of “exact complexity” here is the complexity-class classification used by the source when presenting these gaps. Both problems and the unrestricted priority parameter are preserved. Recognition does not ask for a smallest equivalent automaton, and recent minimization or state-reduction results do not automatically classify it.

cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(N+1)^c\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(N\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.
cards.why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).

The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(N+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That paper does not decide the validity of the separate 2025 algorithm claim.

cards.title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time decider that, given a finite simple stochastic game \(G\), start vertex \(s\) and binary rational \(r\in[0,1]\), accepts exactly when \(v_G(s)>r\)? Here \(v_G(s)=\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\Pr_s^{\sigma,\tau}[\text{eventually reach sink }1]\). Time is measured in the total encoded bit length of the game, start vertex and threshold.
cards.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
cards.why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

cards.context:
This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

The exact branch formerly indexed as TCS-2427 asks for a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm returning optimal positional strategies for a finite, explicitly given, two-player zero-sum turn-based game. Each state is owned by one player; every available action has a rational reward to Max and a rational probability distribution over successor states. Min receives the opposite reward. A common rational discount multiplier \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is part of the binary input, and Max's objective is \(\mathbb E[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_t]\). Multiplication by \(1-\gamma\) leaves optimal strategies unchanged. The factor is constant during a play but may approach one across inputs. Time must be polynomial in the complete encoding length, including \(\gamma\); polynomial dependence on \(1/(1-\gamma)\) alone is insufficient. Exact solving of this class and simple stochastic games are polynomial-time equivalent. The source's additional approximation branch has no precision selected here.

The 2023 source explicitly separates the known constant-discount algorithms from the input-dependent discount question. The checked 2024 paper invokes the reduction of discounted game values and optimal policies to SSGs. These connections motivate consolidating the exact branch into the present threshold problem; they do not establish that its polynomial-time target is solved.

cards.title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm{P}\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm{P}\).
cards.definitions:
The edge set is a subset of \(V\times V\); self-loops are allowed and duplicate edges are not listed. Every listed edge has one arbitrary integer weight, possibly negative or zero. Either ownership set may be empty, and edges may connect vertices of the same owner. There are no chance vertices, additional agents, hidden information, simultaneous moves, fairness constraints, or extra payoff coordinates. Every vertex has a successor, so no finite-play convention is needed.

A finite history from \(s\) is a nonempty vertex sequence \(h=(s=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) following edges of \(E\). A strategy of Max assigns to every such history ending in \(V_{\mathrm{Max}}\) a successor \(v\) with \((v_t,v)\in E\); define a strategy of Min analogously. The sets of these total deterministic history-dependent functions are \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}}\). Neither player sees future choices. A strategy may depend on the complete known instance and entire finite history; the problem statement places no memory or computability restriction on strategies. For any pair, the play is uniquely determined by recursion. A positional strategy means that the selected successor depends only on the current vertex; positional optimality is an established theorem, not an additional promise on the instance.

For \(T\ge1\), set \(a_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\). The lower limit means
\[\liminf_{T\to\infty}a_T=\sup_{N\ge1}\inf_{T\ge N}a_T.\]
It is a finite real number because \(|a_T|\le W\), where \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|)\). The average need not converge for arbitrary history-dependent play. A negative finite prefix is allowed: this objective imposes no lower bound on the running cumulative sum and no prescribed initial energy budget. The payoff is not a discounted sum or a finite-window average.

For a concrete binary encoding, let \(b(u)\) be the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(u\), without leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Define \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Encode an integer \(z\) by \(B(\zeta(z))\), where \(\zeta(z)=2z\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(\zeta(z)=-2z-1\) for \(z<0\). This is a signed binary representation with a uniquely recoverable sign and magnitude; it is not unary in \(|z|\).

The input is \(B(n)B(m)B(s)\), followed by the \(n\) ownership bits in vertex order, and then \(m=|E|\) triples \(B(u)B(v)B(\zeta(w(u,v)))\), listing edges in increasing lexicographic endpoint order. Ownership bit one denotes Max and zero denotes Min. The complete string must satisfy the stated graph and encoding conditions, with no trailing bits. All other binary strings are rejected and are outside \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). Let \(L\) denote the complete input length. Input validation and the translation to ordinary explicit adjacency-list signed-binary representations are polynomial-time operations; these representation conventions do not impose a graph or weight promise.

Membership in \(\mathrm{P}\) means that there are a finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that for every binary string \(x\), \(A(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps, outputting one exactly when \(x\in\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). The same program and constants must work for every size, graph, weight assignment and start vertex. Input reading, validation, arithmetic, storage access and output all count. There is no advice, randomization, game-solving oracle or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily large integers. The polynomial may depend on the fixed program but not on \(n,m,W\) or the instance. The output is only the exact winner bit; the task does not require printing an infinite strategy or play.

There is no bound on \(W\) in terms of \(n\) or \(m\). Its contribution to the input is logarithmic, so a bound polynomial in \(n,m,W\) is pseudopolynomial and need not be polynomial in \(L\). A rational threshold \(a/b\), with binary integers \(a\) and \(b>0\), gives an equivalent decision model: the weights \(bw(e)-a\) have polynomial encoding length and their nonnegative mean threshold expresses the original threshold. Thus fixing the threshold to zero retains the binary-weight complexity question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
 A(x)\text{ halts within }C(|x|+1)^d\text{ steps and outputs }\mathbf1_{\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}}(x),\]
or its logical negation, with the machine and language definitions above. A positive proof must establish the exact game semantics, correctness on every valid instance, rejection of invalid encodings, and the full polynomial bit bound. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, rather than only a particular local-improvement rule, representation, certificate family or algorithmic framework.

A pseudopolynomial bound, a polynomial bound only after random perturbations, a randomized expected-time guarantee, or an algorithm for a restricted graph or weight family does not answer the full question. A polynomial number of arithmetic operations alone is insufficient if intermediate integers require superpolynomial bit length. A strongly polynomial algorithm with polynomially bounded bit representations would suffice but is more than required. There is no approximation tolerance or unproved complexity hypothesis in the target.
cards.why: Mean-payoff games model sustainable long-run rewards when an adversary controls part of a finite system. Their exact winner problem has short certificates for both answers, yet its unrestricted polynomial bit complexity remains an important question in quantitative verification and graph-game theory.

Requiring every partial sum to stay nonnegative is a different objective. A play of weight zero forever is winning here because the threshold is nonnegative, not strictly positive.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players. With both such strategies fixed, a finite graph produces an eventually repeated cycle, whose average determines the payoff. The resulting certificates place the winner language in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): yes and no instances each have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. Zwick and Paterson give the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games, which add random transitions.

cards.title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
cards.formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
cards.definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.
cards.why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.

cards.context:
Presburger arithmetic allows arbitrary first-order quantification but restricts its numerical operations to addition, order and fixed integer coefficients. Adding one decidable predicate can still change decidability of the full theory: the issue is the interaction with unbounded quantifiers, not the cost of evaluating that predicate at a known integer.

The source works over integers and writes an order-based twin-prime sentence. Accordingly, this card includes order and takes primes to be positive. For example, the twin-prime assertion is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\le y\land\mathrm{Pr}(y)\land\mathrm{Pr}(y+2))\).

The source also invokes Goldbach’s conjecture. Its even-input restriction must be explicit: one correct sentence is \(\forall n\,(n\ge2\Rightarrow\exists p\,\exists q\,(\mathrm{Pr}(p)\land\mathrm{Pr}(q)\land p+q=n+n))\). The printed illustrative sentence on p. 29 omits that restriction; the decision question itself does not depend on this typo.

Bateman, Jockusch and Woods prove, assuming the linear case of Schinzel’s hypothesis, that multiplication is definable in the natural-number structure with addition and primes, yielding undecidability. The nonnegative integers are definable in the ordered integer structure, so this conditional obstruction applies to the present target too. The hypothesis is essential to the stated theorem.

Dickson’s prime-tuples conjecture is the assertion that finitely many integer affine forms with positive leading coefficients take simultaneous prime values infinitely often whenever no prime divides their product for every integer argument. The card does not assume this conjecture.

Kaplan and Shelah prove conditional decidability for the unordered additive integer structure whose predicate includes both primes and their negatives. Their introduction explicitly retains the number-theoretic assumption on the ordered undecidability result, although the abstract abbreviates that qualification. The absence of order and the symmetric prime convention are substantive differences.

The 2024 survey explicitly retains the present decision question. The September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; this is dated evidence and a search limit, not a proof that the question remains open.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
cards.why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision directly claims a strongly polynomial algorithm for general LP; Lemma 7.1 asserts a linear bound on its iteration count. A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation. This review has not certified the proof or located independent primary validation in bounded searches.

This review read that note, the theorem and the stated complexity conclusion, without certifying their proof or the full bit-complexity requirements. cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(N\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
cards.definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(N\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.
cards.why: Simplex is a central optimization method whose practical effectiveness has long exceeded its general worst-case guarantees. The question isolates whether exact polynomial-time linear optimization is compatible with its required improving basis exchanges, including degeneracy, and with efficiently choosing every exchange.

cards.context:
General linear programming has polynomial-time algorithms measured in the binary input size. This card imposes the additional requirement that the computation reach its answer through legal simplex pivots on the given program from the supplied basis. The August 2026 full version of the ranking-based paper still poses the unrestricted pivot-rule question as open.

A short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short improving path to an optimum. A polynomial bit-time rule would bound both the number of its basis exchanges and the work required to choose them. Its bound may depend on coefficient bit lengths; it would not by itself establish a strongly polynomial LP algorithm or a polytope diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy allows many bases to represent one point. Kukharenko and Sanità bound consecutive degenerate improving pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n-m-1\), with efficient implementation when an improving feasible direction is available. Their result controls a block of stalling at that vertex; it does not give a dimension-independent or polynomial-in-input bound on the total number of distinct vertices visited by an arbitrary simplex run.

Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a two-phase shadow-vertex simplex method. The expectation is over Gaussian perturbations around an arbitrary input, with polynomial dependence on dimensions and on \(1/\sigma\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the relative perturbation scale. This does not bound the deterministic worst-case bit time on every unperturbed rational input.

The ranking-based results restrict the information a rule may use. One theorem gives a superpolynomial iteration lower bound in \(n\) for index-ranking rules with \(o(n/\log n)\) memory states. The other gives \(\Omega(2^{\sqrt K})\) iterations for the stated memoryless class based only on rankings by index, reduced cost and objective increase, where \(K\) counts nonzero constraint-matrix entries. The definitions also require choices to respect ranking-preserving relabelings. Memory states are not bits of memory, and \(K\) is not this card's binary input length \(N\). These restricted-information theorems do not exclude algorithms with full numerical access and general polynomial-time history.

Disser and Mosis obtain an all-pivot-rules lower bound for the active-set method with higher-degree polynomial objectives on a hypercube. Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen this to convex quadratic maximization. The objective is nonlinear and the optimization direction is maximization; neither theorem is an all-rules lower bound for the linear objective required here.

Black and Steiner’s April 2026 revision proves that finding a shortest monotone pivot sequence is NP-hard, already for simple polytopes where vertices are nondegenerate. Thus a polynomial-time algorithm for always finding a shortest sequence would imply P = NP. This card asks for some polynomial-time legal run and does not require its number of pivots to be minimum, so shortest-path hardness alone does not answer it negatively.

cards.title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm that solves every rational P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial bit time? More precisely, are there a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded rational input
\[n\in\mathbb N_{>0},\qquad M\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad q\in\mathbb Q^n,\]
the machine halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below, and whenever \(M\) is a P-matrix it outputs \(z,w\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying
\[w=Mz+q,\qquad z_i\ge0,\quad w_i\ge0,\quad z_iw_i=0\quad(1\le i\le n)?\]
A P-matrix has strictly positive determinant for every nonempty principal submatrix. No certificate of this promise is supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize it. The constants \(B,k\) and the program are shared by all dimensions and all rational coefficients.
cards.definitions:
Matrix promise. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), the principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) consists of the rows and columns with indices in \(S\), both in increasing order. Thus the promise is
\[\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n],\ \det M[S,S]>0.\]
Here the determinant is the usual alternating sum of products, evaluated exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). Strict positivity is essential. There is no symmetry, sparsity, triangularity, positive-semidefiniteness or nondegeneracy assumption. In particular, a valid solution may have both \(z_i=w_i=0\) in some coordinate.

Equations and output. The matrix product is \((Mz)_i=\sum_{j=1}^nM_{ij}z_j\), and all inequalities use the ordinary rational order. With \(z,w\ge0\), coordinatewise complementarity is equivalent to \(z^Tw=\sum_{i=1}^n z_iw_i=0\). A solution is the complete pair of vectors, with exact rational coordinates. An interval, floating-point vector or small residual is not an exact solution under this task. The guarantee is a search guarantee: returning only a yes/no answer about existence is insufficient.

Binary encoding. To make the bit model definite, encode a nonnegative integer \(t\) by
\[u(t)=1^{b(t)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(t+1),\qquad b(t)=\lfloor\log_2(t+1)\rfloor+1,\]
where \(\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) is its binary expansion without leading zeroes, of length \(b(t)\). The initial run of ones specifies that length. A rational number is written uniquely as \(p/d\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\gcd(|p|,d)=1\), and is encoded by a sign bit, then \(u(|p|)\), then \(u(d)\). The sign bit is zero for nonnegative \(p\), including zero, and one for negative \(p\). Thus zero uses numerator zero and denominator one. The input concatenates \(u(n)\), all \(n^2\) entries of \(M\) in row-major order, and the \(n\) entries of \(q\). Every entry, including a zero entry, is explicitly present. A syntactically valid input has exactly this form and no trailing bits. Its total binary length is \(N\). The output concatenates the \(n\) rational encodings of \(z\), followed by those of \(w\), in index order; \(n\) is already known from the input. Other usual explicit binary rational encodings are polynomially equivalent to this convention.

Computation. The same finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program is used for every input. One transition costs one step. Reading input, rational arithmetic, comparisons, intermediate representations and writing the entire output are all charged. There are no oracles, real-number unit-cost operations, randomness, nonuniform advice or free preprocessing. The polynomial time bound applies to every syntactically valid rational input, including matrices that fail the P-matrix promise. On those nonpromised inputs any halting output is allowed; detecting a violated principal minor is not required. Behavior on malformed input strings is unrestricted. A polynomial bound only on promised inputs is equivalent for this existence question, since a known polynomial bound can be enforced with a clock and arbitrary output after timeout. The bound may depend polynomially on coefficient bit lengths through \(N\); this is not a demand for a strongly polynomial number of arithmetic operations independent of those lengths.

Quantifier order. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists B,k\,\forall(n,M,q)\) with the time guarantee above and correctness whenever \(\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\). Coefficient magnitudes, dimension, degeneracy and numerical conditioning may vary without restriction; they do not permit selecting a different program or polynomial for each input.

cards.context:
Complementarity imposes a discrete choice within linear equations: each coordinate must have \(z_i=0\), or \(w_i=0\), or both. For \(M=I_n\), the solution is \(z_i=\max\{0,-q_i\}\) and \(w_i=\max\{0,q_i\}\). For a general P-matrix, the coordinates interact through \(Mz\), so this coordinate-by-coordinate formula no longer applies.

The classical P-matrix characterization states that the linear complementarity system has exactly one solution for every real right-hand side if and only if all principal minors are positive. Uniqueness concerns the vector pair, not the choice of a complementary basis; degenerate instances can have several bases representing the same solution. The existence and uniqueness theorem does not itself give the polynomial algorithm requested here.

Rational exact output does not require an exponentially long description. In a solution, let \(S=\{i:z_i>0\}\). Then \(z_{[n]\setminus S}=0\), \(w_S=0\), and \(M[S,S]z_S=-q_S\); this principal matrix is nonsingular. Clearing input denominators and applying determinant bounds shows that its rational solution and the resulting \(w\) have polynomial bit length. If \(S\) is empty, \(z=0\) and \(w=q\). The difficult part is finding a valid pattern efficiently.

P-matrix recognition is co-NP-complete, but this card supplies the property as a promise. Gordon and Shu give polynomial conversions between different certificates that a matrix violates the promise. Such certificate results do not make recognition part of this task, and recognition hardness does not prove that promised solution finding is hard.

Fearnley, Gordon, Mehta and Savani place the promised problem in a class based on finding the endpoint of a unique, implicitly represented path whose potential increases along it. Their total-search variants permit a certificate of a violated promise as an alternative output. These complexity-class containments organize the search problem but do not give polynomial-time solution finding. The present card requires a solution only on P-matrix inputs.

Gärtner and Sprecher give polynomial algorithms for Hessenberg P-matrices, which have zero entries beyond the first off-diagonal on one side; tridiagonal matrices are included. Their \(O(n^5)\) arithmetic-operation bound combines polynomially many basis tests with linear-system solves. Exact rational linear algebra gives polynomial bit complexity for these subclasses. The general matrix in this card has no such zero pattern.

The ICALP 2024 paper “Two Choices Are Enough” reduces generalized complementarity instances to the ordinary binary-choice problem and relates them to geometric search problems. This equivalence extends the reach of P-matrix LCP; it is not a polynomial solver for it. ETH’s 2025 activity report continues to list general polynomial-time solution finding as open.

E.-Nagy and Végh’s June 2026 revision gives an algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the input length and in the optimized handicap \(\widehat\kappa^\star(M)\), the best handicap attainable by positive diagonal row scaling. The handicap measures departure from the inequality \(x^TMx\ge0\). Their general upper bound on the unscaled handicap is exponential in input bit complexity, and the algorithmic theorem does not give a polynomial input-length bound on the optimized parameter. It therefore does not settle the all-P-matrix target.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
cards.definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.

cards.context:
A linear program optimizes a linear function over a polyhedron. Moving between adjacent vertices is the geometric operation behind simplex pivots. The conjecture asks whether every pair of feasible vertices is joined by a short sequence of these moves, before any navigation rule or objective is chosen.

The facet count measures the number of essential inequalities. It can be much smaller than the number of vertices: the cube \([0,1]^d\) has \(2d\) facets and \(2^d\) vertices, but diameter only \(d\). Merely bounding distance by the number of vertices therefore does not give the desired polynomial.

A bound such as \(n^d\) allows the exponent to increase with the dimension. The conjecture demands one fixed exponent, and allows neither the multiplicative constant nor that exponent to depend on the particular polyhedron.

Santos’s 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets has diameter greater than 43, refuting the original Hirsch bound \(n-d\) for bounded polytopes. That example was consistent with larger polynomial bounds. The bounded counterexample does not itself show superpolynomial growth.

Todd proves the general bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the single-vertex boundary cases treated separately. The earlier Kalai–Kleitman bound was \(n^{2+\log_2 d}\). These estimates are quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.

Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has exponent \(\log_2 d-\log_2\log d+O(1)\) for large \(d\). The exponent still grows without bound, so this improvement does not establish the conjecture.

The length of the best available path is different from the length of a path selected by a particular pivot rule. A positive answer would give geometric existence, without supplying a fast procedure for choosing the next edge or guaranteeing objective improvement.

Wulf proves that computing diameter is \(\Pi_2^p\)-hard even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, the convex hulls of incidence vectors of perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. This is a hardness classification at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It concerns finding the value, and is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on that value.

Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a circuit-diameter bound \(O(r^2\log r)\) for standard-form polyhedra \(\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank \(r\ge2\). A circuit direction is a nonzero kernel vector whose set of nonzero coordinates contains no smaller support of another nonzero kernel vector. A circuit step moves maximally in a feasible circuit direction and may pass through a higher-dimensional face. Such a walk need not follow graph edges.

A monotone path increases a chosen linear objective. A coherent monotone path is more restricted: it traces optimizers as a second linear objective varies along a line in objective space. Black and Xue’s July 2026 preprint gives polytopes for which every coherent monotone path for the chosen orientation is long. Their restriction is absent from ordinary graph distance.

More precisely, their Theorem 1.1 gives, for each \(q\ge3\), a polytope of dimension \(q+1\) with \((2q+1)(q+1)+1\) facets and an objective for which every coherent monotone path has length at least \(2^{q-1}-1\). The paper continues to list the unrestricted polynomial Hirsch question as open.
