cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
cards.definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
cards.why: Determines whether adaptive computable fair betting detects every effective measure-theoretic failure of randomness in an individual infinite sequence. Equality or separation would connect two foundational ways to formalize unpredictability.

cards.context:
Martin-Löf randomness and betting randomness concern individual infinite objects. Effective tests describe events of arbitrarily small fair-coin probability, while a gambler uses observed bits to determine future bets. Neither definition is a confidence score for a finite sample. Every finite binary string can occur at the start of a Martin-Löf random sequence, so a finite unusual-looking prefix alone cannot settle membership in either class.

Adaptivity changes the information available to a strategy. It may inspect coordinate 100, then choose between coordinates 3 and 7 based on that value. Reading a bit with no money at risk still reveals it and makes it unavailable for later betting. The strategy must choose its next fresh position and wager using only its current history; otherwise it could exploit information it has not legitimately obtained.

The established implications are \(\operatorname{MLR}\subseteq\operatorname{KLR}\subseteq\operatorname{CR}\), where computable randomness \(\operatorname{CR}\) rules out successful total computable fair gamblers that read bits in their original order. The first inclusion is the known direction; the card asks whether it is equality. Kolmogorov–Loveland stochasticity instead controls limiting frequencies of adaptively selected bits and is a different, weaker requirement than defeating all fair betting strategies.

Partiality must be separated from which bits are eventually visited. The standard theory permits partial computations, and using total nonmonotonic procedures yields the same randomness class. However, a total procedure can still leave infinitely many coordinates unseen. Requiring a total strategy to visit every coordinate changes its power: the classical source shows that such a strategy can be matched by a monotonic gambler on every sequence where it succeeds.

Kastermans and Lempp separate Martin-Löf randomness from randomness against predetermined computable permutation orders, and against the more general predetermined computable injective orders. A permutation visits every position; an injection may omit positions. In both cases the query order is fixed independently of revealed bit values. These separations therefore do not decide what fully adaptive strategies can detect.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan show that a Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequence has Martin-Löf random subsequences on computable sets of coordinates with densities arbitrarily close to one. Their Theorem 12 says that splitting at any infinite co-infinite computable set leaves at least one Martin-Löf random part. These are substantial proximity results, but randomness of a subsequence does not establish randomness of the whole interleaving.

Petrović’s universal-pair result concerns a generalized half-betting game. Such games allow richer computable partitions of the remaining possible sequences than asking for the value of one fresh coordinate. A pair of generalized strategies can cover all failures of Martin-Löf randomness, but this theorem does not turn them into strategies in the more restricted query model of the card.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.

cards.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) and one uniform deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol which, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every profile of \(n\) nonatomic additive cake valuations, makes at most \(Cn^d\) queries and produces a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the entire cake satisfying
\[
 \mu_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_j)\qquad\text{for every }1\le i,j\le n?
\]
Every allocated piece may be a finite union of intervals. The allocation must be complete and exactly envy-free on every profile and for every valid choice of cut-query responses.
cards.definitions:
The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent \(i\)'s valuation \(\mu_i\) is an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure: it is nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu_i([0,1])=1\), and \(\mu_i(\{x\})=0\) for every point \(x\). A piece is a finite union of intervals, with endpoints assigned consistently to make the pieces disjoint. Endpoints have zero value for every agent. Measures need not have densities, and there is no bound on density, number of breakpoints or description complexity. No distribution over profiles is assumed.

The protocol receives \(n\) and accesses valuations only through these exact oracles:

\(\operatorname{Eval}(i,x,y)\), for known marks \(0\le x\le y\le1\), returns \(\mu_i([x,y])\).

\(\operatorname{Cut}(i,x,\alpha)\), for a known mark \(x\) and a requested real value \(0\le\alpha\le\mu_i([x,1])\), returns some \(y\in[x,1]\) such that \(\mu_i([x,y])=\alpha\). This returned coordinate becomes a known mark. Initially only \(0\) and \(1\) are known. Nonatomicity guarantees existence of an answer. If an interval has zero value, a cut may have several valid positions; every such response must preserve the guarantee. The protocol must issue only valid queries.

Each evaluation or cut call counts as one query. The protocol may combine interval values by additivity and use previously learned values without paying again. It may query one agent at a mark obtained from another. The final allocation must use endpoints among the known marks; arbitrary newly guessed endpoints are not available as free cuts.

Uniformity means one finite program for all \(n\). Between queries it may use integer computation, store and copy exact real answers, perform real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero number, and compare real numbers exactly. Its program has rational real constants and may perform arbitrary finite loops and finite searches. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; no time, memory or bit-precision bound is imposed on this local computation. It must nevertheless terminate after finitely many operations on every allowed execution. This specifies a query model with exact real arithmetic, not a Turing computation of the digits of arbitrary valuation reals.

The output lists, for each agent, finitely many intervals with known endpoints. Their union covers \([0,1]\), and no interior point belongs to two agents' pieces. Shared boundary points are assigned to one incident piece. Empty pieces are allowed, but no positive-length residue may be discarded, even if all agents value it at zero.

Envy-freeness compares all pieces using the evaluating agent's own measure. It requires every displayed inequality exactly, with no additive or multiplicative fairness error. It does not require a connected piece per agent or impose any incentive-compatibility condition. The query bound is worst-case over both valuation profiles and valid oracle responses. There is no randomization or favorable-profile exception.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one protocol and constants satisfying the statement, with proofs of query validity, termination, complete allocation, exact envy-freeness and the uniform polynomial query bound; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence claim in the specified model.

A protocol with an arbitrary finite bound depending on \(n\), a polynomial average-case or approximate-fairness guarantee, or a protocol leaving cake unallocated is insufficient. A lower bound for one particular procedure does not rule out all polynomial-query protocols. This is an existence question about an exact fairness property and an asymptotic resource bound, so numerical approximation of envy does not meet the answer criterion.
cards.why: The question asks how much preference information is necessary to divide a continuous resource exactly without anyone preferring another person’s share. A polynomial query bound would separate the information needed for fairness from the enormous bounds in existing general protocols.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent two
cards.formal: Does the matrix multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\) equal two? Precisely, writing \(s(n)\) for the minimum arithmetic gate count of an exact circuit multiplying two \(n\times n\) complex matrices, is it true that \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2},\qquad s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}?\] The circuit family and its constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\); an \(O(n^2)\) bound is not required.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required \(n^2\) outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). Use an [arithmetic circuit](definitions.html#arithmetic-circuits) over \(\mathbb C\), with input variables, arbitrary field constants, and binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The binary target is \(\omega=2\), with the positive-slack convention just stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an upper bound \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\) on the specified arithmetic-circuit size over \(\mathbb C\), or show that some positive \(\varepsilon\) admits no such bound.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

cards.title: Logarithmic exponent of integer multiplication
cards.formal:
For a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) that exactly multiplies every pair of \(n\)-bit nonnegative binary integers, let \(t_M(n)\) be its worst-case transition count. Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the logarithmic-overhead exponent
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}=\inf\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists M\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge n_0,\quad t_M(n)\le Cn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\right\}.
\]
The machine model and quantifiers are specified below. The linear factor \(n\) accounts for the bit scale of the input and output; the requested number describes the power of the logarithmic overhead. The output is the exact product, explicitly written in \(2n\) bits. The exponent lies in \([0,1]\); attaining its infimum is not required.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).

The infimum ranges over logarithmic powers attainable as upper bounds by correct machines in this model. For each candidate exponent \(a\), the machine \(M\), multiplicative constant \(C\) and threshold \(n_0\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the input length or input values. One fixed machine must meet each asserted bound at every sufficiently large length and remain correct at all lengths. It is not permissible to minimize separately over a different hardcoded program for each \(n\).

The explicit output requires \(\Omega(n)\) transitions. The known \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm makes the defining set nonempty and gives \(0\le\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1\). This definition neither assumes an ordinary growth limit nor requires one machine to attain the infimum. Exponent zero does not by itself assert a linear-time algorithm: it allows separate upper bounds with arbitrarily small positive powers of \(\log n\). Multiplicative constants and iterated-logarithmic factors are not part of the requested numerical accuracy.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real number \(b\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|b-\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}|\le1/100\), in the stated uniform deterministic multitape model. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint; both endpoints must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. Upper bounds must respect the order of quantifiers: each machine is fixed across all input lengths. A lower bound must cover every correct machine in the model. A lower bound on the infimum does not require an attained optimal time or an eventual matching lower bound at every input length. The answer concerns the logarithmic exponent after the linear factor \(n\), not a polynomial exponent of \(n\), a matching full running-time function, or a rounded estimate without a proved error bound.

cards.context:
For example, \(11_2\) multiplied by \(11_2\) is \(1001_2\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The task scales to arbitrarily long binary inputs. The numerical question measures how much logarithmic overhead is necessary beyond the linear cost of handling the input and output bits.

A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

Harvey and van der Hoeven proved an \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm in the multitape Turing model in 2021. This establishes \(\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1\), but does not determine the optimal exponent. Their 2025 paper records the absence of an unconditional superlinear lower bound in this unrestricted model.

A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

The exponent records the power of \(\log n\) multiplying the linear term. For example, a bound \(n(\log n)^{1/2}\) would give \(\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1/2\). The rates \(n\log n\) and \(n\log n/\log\log n\) both have logarithmic growth exponent one, so distinguishing their iterated-logarithmic factors is outside this target. The infimum convention also avoids assuming that a single optimal machine exists.

cards.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: The question compares unrestricted arithmetic circuits with path-sum computation inside the class of efficiently representable polynomials. Equality would make polynomial-size determinants of affine matrices sufficient to express every polynomial-degree circuit family. Inequality would establish a fundamental separation within efficient algebraic computation, isolating power supplied by general multiplication together with reuse of intermediate results.

cards.context:
Circuits combine previously computed polynomials by both addition and multiplication, with unrestricted reuse. An ABP records sums of products along paths with affine labels. ABPs are polynomially equivalent to skew circuits, where each multiplication gate has at least one operand that is an input variable or constant. The conjectural gap concerns the size of exact representations under these two forms of computation, rather than which individual polynomials can be represented at all.

The polynomial-degree condition is essential. Small general circuits can have output degree exponential in their size, whereas an ABP with affine labels has degree at most its longest source-to-sink path. Such degree alone cannot separate the classes in this card because it is explicitly required to stay polynomial. The stated bounds concern the final polynomial; intermediate cancellations and degrees in a competing circuit are allowed.

Determinants give an equivalent structural description of \(\mathrm{VBP}\): a family belongs to this class exactly when it has representations \(f_n=\det(A_{n,0}+\sum_j x_j A_{n,j})\) with polynomially bounded matrix dimension and complex constant matrices. The determinant itself admits polynomial-size ABPs. Thus \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VBP}\) would make determinants universal for the circuit families in the statement. This is distinct from permanent versus determinant: the permanent is not known to have the polynomial-size general circuits required on the easy side of a separation here.

The classical Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations among formulas, ABPs and circuits for polynomial-degree families. The ITCS 2024 paper recalls that their quasipolynomial versions coincide, where a quasipolynomial bound means \(n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\). A polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is stronger. Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.

Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.

cards.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(K,C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) there is an arithmetic formula \(F_n\) over \(\mathbb C\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{size}(F_n)\le K n^C,\qquad \llbracket F_n\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n(X),\]
where \(\llbracket F_n\rrbracket\) is its output as a formal commutative polynomial and
\[\operatorname{Det}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
The formula is a binary expression tree with arbitrary complex constants and addition, subtraction and multiplication. Computations may use cancellations, but intermediate expressions cannot be shared. The same constants \(K,C\) must work for all dimensions.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameters. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) has \(n^2\) distinct commuting indeterminates as its entries. The positive integer \(n\) is the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. The set \(S_n\) consists of all permutations of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}\), where \(\operatorname{inv}(\pi)\) counts pairs \(i<j\) with \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). All calculations take place in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\). In particular \(\operatorname{Det}_1=x_{11}\); no invertibility or numerical-entry promise is imposed.

Formula syntax and evaluation. A formula is a finite rooted binary tree with ordered children. A leaf is labelled by one input variable or one constant in \(\mathbb C\). Each internal node is labelled \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\) and computes the corresponding operation on the two child polynomials; subtraction uses left child minus right child. The root’s polynomial is denoted \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\). Every node other than the root has exactly one parent. Repeated uses of an expression therefore require separate copies of its entire subtree. No powers, determinants, summations or other compound expressions are primitive gates: any such shorthand in a proposed family must expand to allowed binary nodes.

Size. Every node counts once, including each occurrence of a variable or constant. Equivalently, a leaf has size one and a node with children \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). Distinct leaves carrying the same value count separately. Define
\[L_{\det}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n\}.\]
The set is nonempty by the finite permutation expansion, so this positive-integer minimum exists. The question is whether \(L_{\det}(n)\) is bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). Allowing real constants in a size bound rather than positive integer \(K,C\) would give the same polynomial-boundedness claim.

Constants and nonuniformity. Each constant leaf has unit size regardless of its magnitude, algebraic degree or description length. Constants and the tree may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and complex constants need not be computable or rational. They cannot depend on the values later substituted for input variables. There is no algorithmic or efficiency requirement for generating the family, and no bit-cost bound on its representation: the resource is algebraic tree size. The field \(\mathbb C\) is fixed throughout; the target is not a simultaneous assertion for all fields.

Exact unrestricted computation. The equality at the root is an exact polynomial identity, coefficient by coefficient. Approximation of coefficients, a limit of formulas or correct evaluation only on a restricted input set does not meet it. Division, inverses, comparisons, branching, input-dependent constants and additional input variables are not allowed. There is no restriction on depth, homogeneity, signs or coefficient magnitudes. Intermediate polynomials may have powers or monomials absent from the determinant, provided they cancel in the final identity. A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. The output determinant is multilinear, but the formula is not required to be multilinear at intermediate nodes.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, prove the existence of allowed formula trees for every dimension, their exact determinant identity, and one common polynomial size bound. A uniform construction is welcome but is not required by this nonuniform target. Count all copied subtrees and constant occurrences.

A negative answer must prove
\[\forall K,C\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\det}(n)>K n^C.\]
It must cover arbitrary complex constants and all unrestricted intermediate computations permitted above. Equivalently, for every \(K,C,N\ge1\), there must be some \(n\ge N\) violating that polynomial bound; finitely many exceptional dimensions can always be absorbed into its constant. It is not necessary to prove that every sufficiently large dimension violates every given polynomial, a stronger eventual-growth claim.

A fixed-power lower bound, such as \(\Omega(n^3)\), leaves larger polynomial bounds possible. Lower bounds only for multilinear, homogeneous, symmetric, monotone, bounded-depth, bounded-coefficient or noncommutative computations do not refute the stated unrestricted commutative claim. An exact identity using a small circuit with shared intermediate results is not yet a small formula, and a large size for one particular determinant expansion is not a lower bound for all formulas. A proof conditional on an unresolved separation must keep that assumption explicit and does not settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.

cards.context:
The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The permutation expansion has \(n!\) summands, but this does not prove that every formula is large. A product of short sums may represent many expanded monomials. For example, the \(2\times2\) determinant is \(x_{11}x_{22}-x_{12}x_{21}\), represented by seven nodes in the stated model. The challenge is one size bound for all dimensions, not finding finite expressions for individual matrices. Numerical Gaussian elimination also does not directly answer the symbolic tree-size question: its usual implementation reuses intermediate entries, divides and chooses pivots.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size \(2^{O(\log ^{2} n)}=n^{O(\log  n)}\). This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is complete for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs. Such a program is a directed acyclic graph with a source and sink; affine-linear edge labels are multiplied along paths and the path products are summed. The class \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially many variables, polynomial degree and polynomial-size branching programs, while \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) uses formula trees. Every formula has a polynomial-size branching program, and every such branching program has a polynomial-size determinant representation. Thus the existence claim here is equivalent to \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\).

The larger class \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) permits polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, where gates may have several consumers, while retaining polynomially many variables and polynomial degree. The June 2026 factoring primer records \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) without a known strict containment. It includes recent closure results for factoring formulas and still expressly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved. A positive answer here would identify the first two classes; it would not alone identify either with \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\).

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are \(n^{2}\) independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power \(3/2\) in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, \((x+y)^{2}- x^{2}- y^{2}\) equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries whose determinants still require \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense \(n^{2}\)-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

cards.title: Explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) it outputs all entries of a rational tensor \(T_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) within \(K(n+1)^a\) bit operations, and \[\forall B\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)\ge Bn?\] Here rank is ordinary tensor rank over the complex numbers. Thus the required ratio \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)/n\) tends to infinity, with no prescribed rate.
cards.definitions:
A tensor \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) is the array \((T_{ijk})_{1\le i,j,k\le n}\), regarded as an element of \(\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\) through the usual inclusion of the rationals into the complex numbers. Its ordinary rank is the smallest integer \(r\ge0\) for which there are vectors \(u^{(s)},v^{(s)},w^{(s)}\in\mathbb C^n\), for \(1\le s\le r\), satisfying
\[
T_{ijk}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u^{(s)}_i\,v^{(s)}_j\,w^{(s)}_k
\quad\text{for every }1\le i,j,k\le n.
\]
An empty sum is the zero tensor. The factors in a rank decomposition may be arbitrary complex vectors, although the constructed tensor entries are rational. No symmetry is required. The target is not matrix rank of an array rearrangement, slice rank, border rank, or an asymptotic tensor-power rank.

The machine outputs the \(n^3\) entries in lexicographic order of \((i,j,k)\). Each entry is an explicitly written signed binary integer numerator and positive binary integer denominator, with delimiters. All bits are charged, so their total length and each individual entry's bit length are polynomially bounded in \(n\). A symbolic power, root-of-unity description, unevaluated arithmetic expression or arbitrary real constant is not a rational-entry output under this convention. All input reading, integer arithmetic, preprocessing and output writing count. The finite program and \(K,a\) are independent of \(n\); there is no advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing.

The algorithm is required on every positive integer dimension, and the rank guarantee holds for all sufficiently large dimensions for each \(B\). The integer threshold \(N\) may depend on \(B\) and the fixed family; it is not required to be computed. No rank decomposition, rank value or lower-bound certificate is an output requirement for \(A\); the rank-growth guarantee must instead be established by the submitted proof. Explicitness here means polynomial time in the dimension to write the whole tensor, not a separate polylogarithmic-time entry-query requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of such a finite construction algorithm, its uniform polynomial bit-cost bound and the entire eventual superlinear rank guarantee, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence proof without the construction cost, a fixed constant multiple of the dimension, growth only along an unspecified subsequence, or a conditional lower bound alone does not meet this target. Any growth rate tending to infinity in the displayed normalized rank suffices; a fixed positive power improvement is not required.
cards.why: Tensor rank measures the number of independent bilinear products needed to express a computation. Explicit superlinear-rank families would turn generic hardness into concrete examples and yield lower bounds for the corresponding constant-degree arithmetic computations.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether every bilinear operation attains, in the exponential growth rate of jointly processed copies, the elementary lower bound already visible from matrices. A positive answer would force matrix multiplication exponent two and impose a simple common asymptotic law on all concise tensors. A negative answer would exhibit an obstruction that survives arbitrarily many grouped copies, beyond the familiar difficulty of decomposing a single tensor.

cards.context:
A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.
